q1.attribution: —Historian's account of the Cold War as a global rivalry, 1945–1991
q1.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE way the superpowers competed without fighting each other directly.
parts.b: Explain ONE cause of the Cold War's emergence after 1945.
parts.c: Explain ONE effect of the Cold War on newly independent nations.

sample_answers.a: They competed through proxy wars — Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan — where each side armed local allies instead of risking direct superpower combat.
sample_answers.b: One cause was the power vacuum in Europe and Asia after 1945: with Germany and Japan destroyed, the United States and the Soviet Union each moved to secure their spheres, and their incompatible visions of security turned friction into permanent rivalry.
sample_answers.c: One effect was constrained sovereignty: new nations were pressured to align with one bloc, and leaders who chose neutrality or the 'wrong' side — from Iran's Mossadegh to Chile's Allende — faced coups or interventions.

q1.stimulus: The Cold War was fought everywhere except on the battlefields of its two main rivals. The United States and the Soviet Union never went to war directly — nuclear weapons made that unthinkable — so they competed through proxies (Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan), through aid and alliances (NATO, the Warsaw Pact), and through prestige projects from the space race to the Olympics. For much of the world, the Cold War was not a standoff but an intervention: superpower rivalry shaped who governed from Guatemala to Indonesia.

q2.attribution: —Adapted from President John F. Kennedy, televised address on the Cuban Missile Crisis, October 22, 1962
q2.directions: Use the passage below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Identify ONE action Kennedy announces in the passage.
parts.b: Explain ONE cause of the crisis described in the passage.
parts.c: Explain ONE way the crisis changed Cold War diplomacy afterward.

sample_answers.a: Kennedy announces a naval quarantine of Cuba to stop further Soviet shipments and demands the removal of the missiles already on the island.
sample_answers.b: One cause was the security dilemma in the nuclear age: the Soviets placed missiles in Cuba to offset U.S. missiles in Turkey and protect their Cuban ally, while the United States read the deployment as an intolerable threat.
sample_answers.c: The crisis pushed both sides toward better communication — the Moscow–Washington hotline was installed in 1963 — and toward the first arms-control agreement, the Partial Test Ban Treaty.

q2.stimulus: [Paraphrase of Kennedy's address:] American intelligence has discovered Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba, ninety miles from our shores. I am declaring a naval quarantine of the island. Any missile launched from Cuba will bring full retaliation against the Soviet Union. I call on Chairman Khrushchev to withdraw these weapons.

q3.directions: Use the image below to answer all parts of the question that follows.

parts.a: Describe ONE feature of the Wall shown in the photograph.
parts.b: Explain ONE cause of the Wall's construction in 1961.
parts.c: Explain ONE way the Wall's fall in 1989 symbolized the end of the Cold War.

sample_answers.a: The photograph shows a stark concrete wall topped with a rounded pipe, flanked by guard towers and a cleared patrol strip — a fortified border running through the middle of a city.
sample_answers.b: One cause was the hemorrhage of East Germans fleeing to the West through open Berlin — some 3 million by 1961 — which threatened the East German state's economic and political survival.
sample_answers.c: The Wall was the Cold War's most visible symbol of division; crowds dismantling it by hand showed that the Soviet bloc could no longer command obedience, and German reunification followed within a year.

q3.stimulus: Photograph of the Berlin Wall dividing East and West Berlin: the concrete barrier with guard towers and floodlights, 1961–1989.
